summary: Teaches a nature-of-science idea for ages 9–11: scientific knowledge about dinosaurs has been repeatedly revised as new evidence arrived, so science is evidence-led, self-correcting and provisional rather than a fixed set of facts. Learners examine documented reversals (sluggish scaly tail-draggers to active, often feathered, tail-up animals; the Brontosaurus/Apatosaurus saga; the warm- vs cold-blooded debate), always pairing a changed idea with the evidence that changed it, and learn to judge competing interpretations by weight of evidence from multiple independent sources. The primary activity is an in-role dialogue with a scientist who lived a reversal; a theory-shift simulation, a then-vs-now comparison, and a recall-matching check are preserved as alternatives with distinct purposes.
misconceptions: 'Science is a fixed set of facts that don't change' — knowledge is revised as evidence improves.
'If scientists change their minds, they were wrong / science is unreliable' — revision on evidence is how science works and is a strength.
'Whatever is in the textbook is final truth' — it is the best current explanation, open to revision.
'Scientists just have opinions' — conclusions are constrained by and judged on evidence.
'A single new discovery instantly overturns everything' — change usually reflects accumulating evidence from multiple sources.

activities.title: Interview a palaeontologist who changed their mind
steps: Talk in role with a palaeontologist who began their career picturing dinosaurs as slow, scaly, tail-dragging lizards.
Before the scientist explains, make your own prediction about a disputed feature (for example, were the biggest dinosaurs feathered?), then update your prediction as evidence is presented.

Ask what changed, and have the scientist walk through concrete evidence: Deinonychus, a lightly built, sickle-clawed dinosaur whose skeleton suggested an active, agile animal rather than a sluggish one, then Liaoning fossil slabs with feathers or feather-like filaments preserved around clearly non-bird dinosaurs.

Push back with your own challenge — e.g. 'How do you KNOW those weren't just birds?' — and listen to the scientist reason it out and say honestly what is still argued (were the largest dinosaurs feathered too?).
Optionally interview a second scientist who reads a disputed fossil differently, and decide which case rests on more evidence.
State in your own words one thing scientists used to think, what they think now, and the new evidence that drove the change.
activities.insight: Good science values changing your mind when the evidence calls for it, because following the evidence — not defending old pictures — is what science is (even though some scientists resisted the new ideas at first); today's textbook is the best current answer, not the last word.

activities.title: Weigh the evidence and watch the picture shift
steps: Drop newly discovered fossils onto a balance that weighs two competing hypotheses (e.g. feathered vs scaly, or warm- vs cold-blooded) and watch the 'best current picture' reconstruction update as evidence accrues.
Build a timeline of a single idea (such as dinosaur metabolism) being revised, placing each discovery where it shifted the accepted view.
Contrast an evidence-rich claim with an evidence-poor one and say which deserves more confidence and why.
Explain what new evidence would be needed to tip the balance toward the other hypothesis.
activities.insight: Revision is a reasoned mechanism: the accepted explanation moves as evidence accumulates, and the best-supported idea is the one that fits the evidence best — weighing both how much there is and how good it is — especially when several independent sources agree.

activities.title: Then-vs-now: tap to reveal what changed and why
steps: Compare an older reconstruction with today's reconstruction of the same animal (e.g. an early-1900s tail-dragging Apatosaurus/'Brontosaurus' mount, or a featherless Deinonychus from the late 1960s–70s) using paired images or a slider.
Tap individual features (posture, tail position, skin/feathers, build) to reveal what changed and the specific evidence that drove each change.
Write a sentence for one feature linking the old picture, the new picture, and the evidence between them.
activities.insight: Each visible change in how we draw dinosaurs was driven by specific evidence, often several lines of it together (such as skeletons, trackways and feather impressions) — revision is reasoned, not arbitrary.

activities.title: Match the evidence to the idea it changed
steps: Match each piece of new evidence (e.g. a feathered theropod slab, a corrected skull) to the specific idea about dinosaurs it revised.
After matching, say in a sentence whether the change was driven by one clue or by several lines of evidence.
Answer the trust question in your own words: 'If scientists keep changing their minds about dinosaurs, how can we trust them at all?'
activities.insight: Recall of specific then/now changes and their driving evidence supports, but does not replace, understanding that revision is how science earns trust.

checkQuestion: Scientists once pictured dinosaurs as sluggish, scaly, cold-blooded reptiles; now many are shown as active, feathered, and possibly warm-blooded. Some people say, 'If scientists keep changing their minds about dinosaurs, how can we trust them at all?' How would you answer that?
checkAnswer: Strong reasoning treats changing ideas as a STRENGTH, not a failure: scientific knowledge updates as new fossils and new methods (feather fossils, CT scans, bone histology) give better evidence. The same fossil can be interpreted differently, so the explanation to trust is the one backed by the most evidence from several independent sources. Trust comes from evidence and self-correction, not from never changing one's mind.
